c1:p0: This is the opening declaration by Thomas Gradgrind, the strict utilitarian schoolmaster, establishing the central philosophy of the novel: the exclusive importance of facts and empirical knowledge, rejecting imagination, emotion, and other forms of learning. This manifesto introduces Gradgrind's rigid educational approach and his character as an uncompromising advocate for factual instruction.
c1:p1: This is the physical description of Mr. Gradgrind, the schoolmaster who has just delivered an impassioned speech insisting that children be taught only "Facts" and nothing else. The passage uses vivid, satirical imagery to characterize him as a rigid, austere figure whose very appearance—his square features, hard expressions, and angular physique—embodies his obsession with facts and rejection of imagination and emotion.
c1:p2: This chunk is a repetition of the protagonist's central doctrine about education, emphasizing his obsessive belief that only factual knowledge matters in life. It appears after a detailed physical description that uses metaphors of hardness and rigidity to reinforce his inflexible, fact-driven character and teaching philosophy.
c1:p3: This passage appears at the end of the opening scene of Hard Times, where Mr. Gradgrind has just finished his passionate declaration about the importance of teaching only Facts. The three adults—Gradgrind, the schoolmaster, and a third person—now survey the students before them, metaphorically viewing the children as empty vessels ready to be filled with factual knowledge. This image reinforces Gradgrind's rigid educational philosophy and establishes the dehumanizing approach to learning that will be central to the novel's critique of Victorian utilitarianism.

c10:p2: Stephen Blackpool is stopped by an old woman from the country who has traveled to Coketown. She asks if he has just come from Mr. Bounderby's house, beginning a curious conversation where she reveals she comes to town once a year to glimpse the gentleman.

c10:p8: Stephen Blackpool encounters an old woman from the country who has come to Coketown to see Mr. Bounderby. She questions Stephen about the gentleman's appearance and health, asking if he looked portly, bold, outspoken, hearty, and healthy.

c10:p10: Stephen Blackpool encounters an elderly country woman on the street near Mr. Bounderby's house. After she inquires about the gentleman and Stephen confirms he has just seen him looking healthy and robust, she expresses her gratitude with these words of contentment.

c10:p12: Stephen Blackpool encounters an old woman from the country who has come to Coketown to see Mr. Bounderby. c10:p14: Stephen Blackpool responds to an old woman from the country who has just told him she makes an annual journey of forty miles by train and walks nine miles each way to visit Coketown and see the gentlemen, particularly Mr. Bounderby. c10:p15: An old country woman explains to Stephen Blackpool that she visits Coketown once yearly, spending her savings to walk the streets and see the wealthy gentlemen, including Mr. Bounderby, whom she has been waiting to observe.
c10:p16: Stephen encounters an old woman from the country who has traveled to Coketown specifically to catch a glimpse of Mr. Bounderby. When she explains she comes once a year just to see the gentlemen of the town, Stephen expresses surprise at her unusual interest.
c10:p17: Stephen Blackpool encounters an old woman from the country who has traveled to Coketown for her annual visit to glimpse Mr. Bounderby. c10:p18: Stephen Blackpool encounters an old woman from the country who has traveled to Coketown solely to glimpse Mr. Bounderby, a gentleman she admires. c10:p21: Stephen Blackpool encounters an old country woman outside Mr. Bounderby's house. She asks if he is happy, and he responds evasively, unwilling to burden her with knowledge of his domestic troubles despite his deep unhappiness caused by his troubled marriage.
c10:p22: Stephen Blackpool encounters an elderly countrywoman outside Mr. Bounderby's house. After she questions him about the gentleman and learns he works at the factory, she asks if he is happy. c10:p23: Stephen Blackpool responds evasively to an old country woman who has asked if he is happy, downplaying his troubles at home while speaking with her on the streets of Coketown before heading to his factory work.

c10:p26: Stephen Blackpool encounters an unusual old woman from the country who questions him about Mr. Bounderby. c10:p27: Stephen Blackpool encounters an elderly woman from the country who has come to Coketown to catch a glimpse of Mr. Bounderby. c10:p29: Stephen Blackpool encounters an old woman from the country who has come to Coketown to see Mr. Bounderby. c10:p30: Stephen Blackpool, a factory worker, encounters an elderly woman from the country who has come to Coketown to glimpse Mr. Bounderby. c10:p33: Stephen Blackpool, a factory worker in Coketown, encounters an elderly country woman who admires Mr. Bounderby. c10:p35: Stephen Blackpool, a factory worker in Coketown, encounters an elderly country woman who asks about Mr. Bounderby. c10:p36: Stephen Blackpool, a factory worker tormented by his unhappy marriage and his love for the patient Rachael, wanders through the rain after work consumed by despair about his trapped circumstances. c11:p0: Stephen Blackpool arrives at his home late at night to find his estranged wife—a neglected, degraded woman—still alive despite her years of abandonment and dissolution. c11:p1: Stephen Blackpool returns home after his troubled nighttime walk to find his estranged wife, who has abandoned him, dying. He enters his modest home with dread and apprehension, unaware that Rachael has been caring for his wife throughout the night.
c11:p2: Stephen returns home late at night to find his wife—an alcoholic outcast whom he abandoned—being cared for by Rachael, a compassionate woman from his past. c11:p3: Stephen Blackpool returns home late at night to find his wife, a dissolute alcoholic, has been brought home injured and delirious. c11:p4: Rachael checks on Stephen's wife, who lies ill and unconscious in the bed, before speaking to Stephen about her condition and care.
c11:p5: Stephen returns home late at night to find Rachael tending to his wife, who has been brought home injured and delirious. Rachael greets him with these words after he has been walking outside in the rain and wind, struggling with despair over his wife's condition and the injustices of life.
c11:p6: Stephen returns home late at night to find his wife in a deteriorated state. When Rachael, who has been caring for his wife, comments that he is very late, he explains that he has been walking outside in the rain and wind, unable to settle his troubled mind.
c11:p7: Rachael comments on Stephen's late-night wandering during harsh weather, noting the heavy rain and wind outside as she tends to his ill wife.
c11:p8: Stephen Blackpool returns home late at night to find his wife—an alcoholic and social outcast—being cared for by Rachael, a compassionate woman who had been his friend before he married. c11:p9: Rachael explains to Stephen why she is at his home nursing his wife, who has arrived in a degraded and injured state. She describes being summoned by the landlady to care for Stephen's wife, who is disoriented, wounded, and bruised from her abandonment and suffering.
c11:p10: Stephen has just returned home to find Rachael caring for his wife, who has been brought home injured and delirious after wandering the streets. As Rachael explains how she came to help and references his merciful nature, Stephen becomes emotionally overwhelmed and sits down in despair.
c11:p11: Stephen returns home late at night to find his wife in a deteriorated state. Rachael, his virtuous friend, has been caring for his wife through the night. c11:p12: Stephen Blackpool sits in despair as Rachael tends to his wife, who has become a destitute alcoholic. c11:p13: Rachael appeals to Stephen's mercy and compassion, urging him to help care for his dying wife despite her past infidelities and moral failings. c11:p14: Stephen's emotional response to Rachael's compassionate care for his suffering wife. c11:p15: Rachael comforts Stephen after finding his wife in a degraded state. She has come to care for the woman despite her abandonment of Stephen, and speaks these words to affirm her loyalty and compassion toward Stephen himself, whom she views as the true victim of his wife's debauchery.
c11:p16: Rachael tends to Stephen's wife with care and mercy, treating wounds on her neck while keeping her screened from Stephen's view. c11:p20: Rachael urges Stephen to rest while she watches over his wife, who lies ill in bed after being found wandering and injured. Rachael has been nursing her and will continue to do so until three in the morning, insisting that Stephen needs sleep more than she does.

c11:p23: Stephen returns home to find his wife—an alcoholic and outcast—being cared for by Rachael, a compassionate woman. c11:p27: Stephen Blackwood, returning home to find his wife being cared for by Rachael, is suddenly gripped by terror when he notices a bottle of poison on the table. c11:p29: Stephen recoils from Rachael's compassionate approach as he becomes distressed upon recognizing a poison bottle on the table beside his wife's bed, fearing what desperation might have driven him to do.
c11:p30: Stephen, deeply distressed after seeing a bottle of poison on the table near his wife's bed, becomes overwhelmed with emotion. c11:p31: Stephen Blackpool, returning home to find his alcoholic wife in a desperate state, is comforted by Rachael's selfless care and compassion. c11:p33: Stephen, exhausted and traumatized after finding his wife neglected, returns home to find Rachael tenderly caring for her. c11:p34: This passage is Stephen Blackpool's vivid nightmare dream. After returning home to find Rachael tending to his abandoned, alcoholic wife, Stephen falls asleep in exhaustion. c11:p35: This chunk is the second part of Stephen Blackpool's traumatic nightmare. c11:p36: Stephen awakens from a troubled dream in which he witnessed his wife's death and was condemned to eternal separation from Rachael. c11:p56: Stephen Blackpool, a mill worker, has returned home to find his estranged wife in a desperate state. c11:p57: Stephen's wife has attempted suicide by poison while Rachael watched over her. c11:p59: Stephen, returning home to find his wife near death after an overdose, has been comforted by Rachael, who saved her life by preventing her from drinking poison. c11:p60: Stephen expresses his profound gratitude and devotion to Rachael after she has saved his wife's life by preventing her suicide attempt with poison. c11:p61: Stephen Blackpool, a mill worker tormented by his abusive wife's addiction, has spent the night watching over her as she recovers from injuries. c11:p62: This passage closes the chapter. Stephen stands in the road after Rachael leaves his home following the night she spent caring for his poisoned wife. c12:p0: This is the opening passage of the chapter, establishing Time as a central metaphor that governs life in Coketown. It compares the passage of time to industrial machinery, reflecting the novel's critique of utilitarian society while suggesting that natural seasons provide the only relief from the town's monotonous uniformity. This passage sets the thematic framework for the subsequent narrative of how time transforms the Gradgrind children—Louisa, Thomas, and Sissy—into adulthood.
c12:p1: This quote marks the beginning of a time-passage sequence showing how Mr. Gradgrind observes his children aging. It introduces Louisa's transition from childhood to womanhood, paralleling similar observations he makes about his son Thomas, before the narrative reveals Mr. Gradgrind's intentions regarding her future marriage arrangement with the wealthy manufacturer Bounderby.
c12:p2: This passage describes how Time, personified as an industrious force, has caused young Thomas Gradgrind to grow noticeably taller since his father last paid attention to him. It follows Mr. Gradgrind's observation that his daughter Louisa is becoming a young woman, and precedes his similar remark about Thomas becoming a young man. The passage uses industrial metaphors to illustrate the passage of time and its transformative effects on the Gradgrind children.
c12:p3: The observation comes as Time metaphorically works on Thomas Gradgrind, transforming him from a boy into a young man. Mr. Gradgrind notices his son has grown a foot taller, leading to this remark about Thomas's development. This mirrors an earlier similar comment about his daughter Louisa, establishing a pattern of time's passage on the Gradgrind children within the industrial setting of Coketown.
c12:p4: This passage describes Thomas Gradgrind's rapid maturation into young manhood while working at Bounderby's mill. Rather than reacting with distress, Mrs. Sparsit responds with patronizing sympathy and superiority, which disconcerts Bounderby. He responds with barely concealed resentment to her condescending wishes for his happiness.
c14:p15: Mrs. Sparsit responds with condescending affability to Mr. Bounderby's announcement of his intention to marry Louisa Gradgrind, subtly asserting her superior position while appearing sympathetic to what she regards as his inferior match.
c14:p16: Mr. Bounderby informs Mrs. Sparsit of his engagement to Louisa Gradgrind. Rather than being distressed, Mrs. Sparsit responds with condescending pity and superiority, which disconcerts Bounderby. He awkwardly proposes that she move to the Bank as its keeper, which she graciously accepts while maintaining her air of compassionate forbearance toward him.
c14:p17: Bounderby has just announced to Mrs. Sparsit that he intends to marry Louisa Gradgrind. After she responds with condescending compassion rather than distress, Bounderby now tactfully suggests that she should leave her position in his household, while offering her an alternative position at the Bank.
c14:p18: Bounderby has just informed Mrs. Sparsit of his engagement to Louisa Gradgrind and suggested she might wish to leave his household. Mrs. Sparsit responds with condescending sympathy, refusing to remain but accepting his offer of a position at the Bank, which she frames as maintaining her social standing while accepting his support.
c14:p19: Bounderby proposes a new living arrangement to Mrs. Sparsit after announcing his engagement to Louisa Gradgrind. He offers her apartments at the Bank as keeper of the place, suggesting she maintain her social position while remaining in his employ.
c14:p20: Mr. Bounderby is informing Mrs. Sparsit of his engagement to Louisa Gradgrind. When he mentions offering her a position at the Bank with "the same terms," Mrs. Sparsit corrects him, reminding him of his prior promise to use the phrase "annual compliment" instead of "terms" when referring to her salary or compensation.
c14:p21: Mr. Bounderby is offering Mrs. Sparsit a position as keeper of the Bank apartments with the same annual salary (which she has corrected him to call "annual compliment" rather than "terms"), asking if she would accept this arrangement so she can remain in his employ after his marriage to Louisa Gradgrind.
c14:p22: Mr. Bounderby has just announced his engagement to Louisa Gradgrind and offers Mrs. Sparsit a position as keeper of apartments at the Bank to replace her current role at his house. Mrs. Sparsit responds graciously to his proposal, concerned about maintaining her social standing.
c14:p23: Mr. Bounderby is reassuring Mrs. Sparsit that the position he is offering her at the Bank is socially appropriate. He is negotiating the terms of her employment there after announcing his engagement to Louisa Gradgrind, and Mrs. Sparsit has expressed concern about not descending in social status by accepting the position.
c14:p24: Mrs. Sparsit responds graciously to Mr. Bounderby's offer of a position as keeper of apartments at the Bank following his marriage announcement. She acknowledges his thoughtfulness in ensuring the position would not lower her social standing, and accepts his generous terms regarding private apartments, provisions, and staff.
c14:p25: Mr. Bounderby is offering Mrs. Sparsit a position as keeper of the apartments at the Bank following his announcement of his engagement to Louisa Gradgrind. He is outlining the comfortable living arrangements and privileges she will receive if she accepts the position.
c14:p26: **Context:** Mrs. Sparsit gracefully accepts Mr. Bounderby's offer of a position as keeper of the Bank apartments after he announces his engagement to Louisa Gradgrind. Despite initially appearing distressed, she responds with dignified composure and condescending compassion, maintaining her superior demeanor while agreeing to leave his household.
c14:p27: After Bounderby announces his engagement to Louisa Gradgrind and offers Mrs. Sparsit a position at the Bank with comfortable terms, she graciously accepts. Rather than being upset or leaving as Bounderby feared, she adopts a position of superior compassion toward him, treating him as a pitiable victim of his own circumstances. Her polite, obliging demeanor and air of sympathetic pity—rather than any emotional outburst—becomes her enduring response to his marriage, making Bounderby deeply uncomfortable despite his attempts to assert himself.
c14:p28: Mr. Bounderby has just informed Mrs. Sparsit of his engagement to Louisa Gradgrind. After resolving the matter with Mrs. Sparsit—who responds with condescending compassion rather than the emotional outburst he feared—Bounderby arranges a position for her at the Bank. The narrative then shifts to describe the eight-week betrothal period leading up to the wedding, emphasizing how the engagement is treated as a purely factual, commercial transaction devoid of romantic sentiment, in keeping with the Gradgrind philosophy of reason and utility.
c14:p29: Mr. Bounderby announces his engagement to Louisa Gradgrind to Mrs. Sparsit, who responds with condescending compassion. After eight weeks of preparations treating the marriage as a business transaction of facts and statistics, Bounderby and Louisa are married in the church at Coketown and return to Stone Lodge for breakfast.
c14:p30: This passage describes the wedding breakfast guests at Louisa Gradgrind and Mr. Bounderby's marriage ceremony. It emphasizes how the assembled party reflects the utilitarian philosophy of the Gradgrind household, with guests who are obsessed with facts, statistics, and practical knowledge rather than sentiment or tradition. The description satirizes their intellectual pretensions and lack of emotional depth.
c14:p31: Mr. Bounderby marries Louisa Gradgrind in a ceremony devoid of romantic sentiment, attended by an "improving party" of rational-minded guests. After the wedding breakfast at Stone Lodge, Bounderby delivers a speech to the assembled company, characteristically boasting about his self-made success and expressing satisfaction with his marriage to the daughter of his friend Tom Gradgrind.
c14:p32: Bounderby's wedding speech at the breakfast following his marriage to Louisa Gradgrind, where he characteristically boasts about his humble origins and independence while claiming to be worthy of his bride.
c14:p33: This passage marks the conclusion of Louisa Gradgrind and Mr. Bounderby's wedding day. After Bounderby delivers a speech at the wedding breakfast at Stone Lodge, the newlyweds prepare to depart for a honeymoon trip to Lyons, where Bounderby intends to inspect the working conditions of factory laborers. As Louisa descends the stairs in her traveling clothes, she encounters her brother Tom, who congratulates her on the marriage with somewhat forced cheerfulness.
c14:p34: The chunk occurs at the end of Louisa's wedding day to Mr. Bounderby. As the newlyweds prepare to depart for their honeymoon trip to Lyons, Tom Gradgrind (Louisa's brother) waits for his sister at the bottom of the stairs and praises her for agreeing to the marriage, which he clearly sees as beneficial to the family.
c14:p35: Louisa shows rare emotion while saying goodbye to her brother Tom on her wedding day, as she departs with her new husband Mr. Bounderby for their honeymoon trip to Lyons.
c14:p36: Tom bids farewell to his sister Louisa at the conclusion of her wedding day, as she and her new husband Mr. Bounderby depart for their honeymoon trip to Lyons by railroad. Tom expresses his approval of her marriage and their new arrangement.
c15:p0: This opening sentence introduces the setting of the chapter—a rare sunny day in the industrial town of Coketown—and establishes the contrast between the harsh industrial environment and occasional natural beauty that will be developed throughout the passage.
c15:p1: This passage describes Coketown's appearance from a distance on a sunny midsummer day, emphasizing the town's obscuring haze of industrial smoke and soot that makes it invisible despite its massive presence—establishing the novel's critical portrayal of industrial pollution and the town's oppressive atmosphere.
c15:p2: This passage, appearing early in the chapter, provides satirical commentary on the fragility and entitlement of Coketown's factory owners (millers). It describes how they claim to be "ruined" by minimal regulations—such as child labor laws, factory inspections, and pollution controls—and their use of threats to resist accountability, particularly their threat to relocate their property abroad when faced with any demands for responsibility.
c15:p3: This chunk follows Dickens's satirical description of Coketown industrialists' threats to relocate their property to the Atlantic if held accountable for labor regulations and safety inspections. It concludes the passage by ironically noting that despite their patriotic rhetoric, the factory owners have never actually followed through on their threats and have instead carefully maintained and expanded their industrial holdings in the town.
c15:p4: This passage is the opening of a detailed description of Coketown on a hot summer day, depicting the oppressive industrial landscape and working conditions. It comes early in the chapter (paragraph 4) and establishes the sensory atmosphere of the factory town—its heat, smoke, oil, and the relentless mechanical rhythms of the mills—before introducing the character Mrs. Sparsit and the arrival of a mysterious gentleman visitor later in the chapter.
c15:p5: This passage describes the oppressive summer heat and industrial pollution of Coketown on a midsummer day. It follows Dickens's depiction of the town's machinery and working conditions, presenting the sun itself as corrupted and harmful by the town's sordid industrialization. The chunk emphasizes how Coketown's industrial character transforms even natural blessings like sunlight into sources of death rather than life.
c15:p6: This passage introduces Mrs. Sparsit at the Bank during a hot summer afternoon. It establishes her role as a respectable presence in the banking establishment, her daily routine of observing Mr. Bounderby from her window, and her pitying attitude toward his marriage to Louisa Gradgrind a year prior. This section sets up her character before she receives an unexpected visitor seeking Mr. Bounderby's address.
c15:p7: This passage describes the Bank building in Coketown where Mrs. Sparsit works as an employee under Mr. Bounderby's patronage. It appears immediately after the description of the oppressive summer heat in the town and before Mrs. Sparsit's introduction in her afternoon apartment at the Bank, establishing the physical setting for her domestic activities and her role as guardian of the Bank's office.
c15:p8: Mrs. Sparsit, a widow employed at the Bank, uses her afternoon presence in the office to maintain an inflated sense of her own importance and social superiority. She views herself as bringing refinement to the commercial space through her genteel appearance and needlework, while the townspeople perceive her alternately as a decorative "Bank Fairy" or a vigilant "Bank Dragon" guarding financial treasures.
c15:p9: Mrs. Sparsit's self-important delusions about her role at the Bank. She imagines herself as guardian of valuable treasures and maintains strict authority over the bank's contents and staff, though the actual items under her watch—worn pens, scraps of paper, fire-buckets—reveal the emptiness of her pretensions.
c15:p10: This chunk describes the staff under Mrs. Sparsit's authority at the Bank in Coketown. It introduces the deaf serving-woman and light porter as her subordinates, characterizing the town's callous attitudes toward the working poor through the dark humor of rumors about the servant's expected murder for her savings. This passage reveals the cruelty and moral decay of Coketown society while establishing the hierarchy and dynamics within the Bank where Mrs. Sparsit holds her position of authority.
c15:p11: This passage describes Mrs. Sparsit taking her afternoon tea at the Bank after office hours, with the light porter Bitzer serving her. It marks the beginning of her conversation with Bitzer about the day's events and the workers of Coketown, before an unexpected visitor arrives seeking Mr. Bounderby's address.
c15:p12: Mrs. Sparsit receives her tea from the light porter Bitzer in the Bank's board-room on a hot summer afternoon, initiating a conversation where she learns about the workers' unrest and discusses an individual employee's poor conduct and improvidence.
c15:p13: Bitzer, the light porter at the Bank, responds to Mrs. Sparsit's thanks. The narrative notes his physical lightness and references his past as a student who defined a horse in a classroom setting, establishing his character as someone shaped by utilitarian education.
c15:p14: Mrs. Sparsit is at the Bank in the late afternoon, having tea with the light porter Bitzer. She asks him if all the Bank's premises have been secured for the day, beginning a conversation about the state of affairs in Coketown.
c15:p15: Mrs. Sparsit asks Bitzer, the light porter, to confirm that the Bank has been closed for the day after office hours. This is part of their routine evening conversation in the Bank's board-room.
c15:p16: Mrs. Sparsit, seated in her afternoon apartment at the Bank, begins her customary conversation with Bitzer, the light porter, asking him about current events in Coketown. She inquires about the workers' activities, particularly their union organizing efforts, which she views with disapproval.
c15:p17: Bitzer, the light porter at the Bank, responds to Mrs. Sparsit's inquiry about the day's news, dismissing the factory workers ("our people") as inherently troublesome while reporting no significant incidents.
c15:p18: Mrs. Sparsit, seated in the Bank office during afternoon hours, inquires of Bitzer, the light porter and informant, about the activities of the town's working class and their labor organizing efforts.
c15:p19: This chunk is Bitzer's response to Mrs. Sparsit's question about what the workers of Coketown are doing. He reports that the laborers continue their attempts at collective organization and solidarity through unions and mutual aid agreements, which Mrs. Sparsit views with disapproval as dangerous class combinations that threaten the established order.
c15:p20: Mrs. Sparsit, sitting in her apartment at the Bank on a summer afternoon, is conversing with Bitzer, the light porter who serves as a spy and informer. She is criticizing the workers of Coketown for their attempts to unite and form labor combinations, expressing her view that the factory masters should prevent such organizing.
c15:p21: Bitzer, the light porter at the Bank, agrees with Mrs. Sparsit's disapproving assessment of the working classes' lack of provident behavior and their tendency to combine together seeking better conditions. This occurs during their afternoon conversation in the Bank office as she takes her tea.
c15:p22: Mrs. Sparsit, who works at the Bank in Coketown, is discussing labor unions and worker organizing with Bitzer, the light porter. She expresses her view that the united factory masters should refuse to employ any workers who participate in union activities or class combinations, thereby breaking the workers' solidarity.
c15:p23: Mrs. Sparsit suggests that the united masters should refuse to employ any workers who are united with other workers. Bitzer responds that the masters have attempted this strategy, but their effort to blacklist unionized workers failed.
c15:p24: Mrs. Sparsit and the bank porter Bitzer are having a confidential conversation in her afternoon room at the Bank. Bitzer is reporting on the day's events and mentions that the working people of Coketown are uniting and forming class combinations. Mrs. Sparsit responds with this statement, asserting that despite her lack of expertise in such matters due to her genteel background, she believes the workers must be subjugated.
c15:p25: Mrs. Sparsit and Bitzer discuss labor unrest in Coketown. She argues that united factory masters should refuse to employ workers who organize together, asserting that the workers "must be conquered." Bitzer defers to her judgment with this statement of agreement and respect.
c15:p26: Bitzer, the light porter and informant at the Bank, prepares for his regular confidential conversation with Mrs. Sparsit by pretending to arrange office supplies while she drinks tea and watches the street below.
c15:p27: Mrs. Sparsit, who supervises the Bank in Coketown, is having her afternoon tea after office hours. She engages in conversation with Bitzer, the light porter who serves as a general spy and informer for the establishment. This question about the day's business is part of their regular confidential chat.
c15:p28: Mrs. Sparsit questions Bitzer, the light porter and spy at the Bank, about the day's events. Bitzer occasionally addresses her as "my lady" instead of "ma'am" as a sign of respect for her aristocratic pretensions, despite her widowed state and current employment at the Bank.
c15:p29: Mrs. Sparsit inquires about the trustworthiness and work habits of the Bank clerks during her afternoon conversation with Bitzer, the light porter, as she takes tea in the Bank office on a hot summer day in Coketown.
c15:p30: Bitzer responds to Mrs. Sparsit's question about whether the Bank clerks are trustworthy, punctual, and industrious, indicating there is one exception to their reliability—likely referring to Tom Gradgrind, whom he will soon criticize as dissipated and idle.
c15:p31: This passage provides Dickens's satirical character sketch of Bitzer, the light porter at the Bank, revealing his cold utilitarianism, moral hypocrisy, and ruthless adherence to economic self-interest. It appears after Mrs. Sparsit notes Bitzer's exceptional "principle" and immediately precedes their conversation about the workers' improvidence, where Bitzer's character becomes instrumental to the chapter's critique of laissez-faire ideology.
c15:p32: Mrs. Sparsit questions Bitzer about the trustworthiness and punctuality of the clerks at the Bank. Bitzer responds that they are generally reliable, but notes there is "the usual exception"—referring to an individual (whom Mrs. Sparsit forbids him to name directly) whom he considers a dissipated, extravagant idler unworthy of his position.
c15:p33: Mrs. Sparsit is taking tea in the Bank office after hours when the light porter Bitzer reports on the day's events. She responds with disapproval to his mention of workers organizing and combining together, shaking her head over her tea as she listens to his concerns about labor unrest in Coketown.
c15:p34: Bitzer, the light porter at the Bank, is reporting to Mrs. Sparsit about the clerks and staff. He expresses his suspicion and disapproval of "Mr. Thomas," a dissipated and extravagant idler who works at the Bank, suggesting he is unworthy and only remains employed due to his connection to someone in authority.
c15:p35: Mrs. Sparsit reprimands Bitzer for mentioning the name "Mr. Thomas" when discussing a clerk at the Bank. She insists that names connected to Mr. Bounderby should not be mentioned under his roof, as she holds a position of trust under him and must remain scrupulously loyal to her patron.
c15:p36: Bitzer apologizes to Mrs. Sparsit after she corrects him for mentioning "Mr. Thomas" by name, reminding him of her earlier instruction to avoid using names in conversation, particularly those connected to Mr. Bounderby's household.
c15:p37: Mrs. Sparsit rebukes Bitzer for mentioning "Mr. Thomas" by name in the Bank, asserting her loyalty to her patron Mr. Bounderby and refusing to allow names connected with him to be spoken under the Bank's roof, citing her sense of honor and moral duty.
c15:p38: Mrs. Sparsit corrects Bitzer for using the name "Mr. Thomas" when referring to an individual employee, reminding him of her duty to her patron Mr. Bounderby. Bitzer apologizes and acknowledges her preference to avoid using names.
c15:p39: Mrs. Sparsit corrects Bitzer for mentioning a name she finds objectionable—Mr. Thomas—insisting he refer to the person only as "an individual" out of loyalty to her patron Mr. Bounderby, to whom the individual is unfortunately connected.
c15:p40: Mrs. Sparsit has just corrected Bitzer for using the name "Mr. Thomas," insisting he refer to Bounderby's dissolute son as "an individual" instead, as she considers herself scrupulously loyal to her patron Bounderby. Bitzer acknowledges this correction and restates his criticism using the approved term.
c15:p41: Mrs. Sparsit corrects Bitzer for using the name "Mr. Thomas" when discussing an individual employee at the Bank, insisting he refer to the person as "an individual" to protect her patron Mr. Bounderby's reputation. After Bitzer complies and resumes his criticism of this improvident employee, Mrs. Sparsit repeats her characteristic sympathetic gestures—sighing and shaking her head over her tea—to indicate she is resuming their conversation about the employee's moral failings.
c15:p42: Bitzer, the light porter and informant at the Bank, is reporting to Mrs. Sparsit about an individual (Tom Gradgrind) who works at the Bank. Bitzer is criticizing this person's character and behavior as idle and extravagant, suggesting he only maintains his position due to his family connections to Mr. Bounderby.
c15:p43: Mrs. Sparsit responds with disapproval to Bitzer's report that Tom Gradgrind (referred to as "an individual" to avoid naming him directly) is a dissipated, extravagant idler who relies on his connection to Mr. Bounderby for support, while she expresses pity for those he is connected to.
c15:p44: Bitzer, the Bank's light porter and informer, is gossiping with Mrs. Sparsit about an unnamed individual (Tom Gradgrind) whom he suspects of being a dissipated idler. In this passage, Bitzer expresses concern that Tom's family connections—particularly his relation at court—may continue to financially support his wasteful lifestyle, implying that Mr. Bounderby's money would ultimately be funding Tom's excesses.
c15:p45: Mrs. Sparsit and Bitzer discuss the poor behavior and improvidence of the working classes and an unnamed individual employed at the bank. Bitzer expresses concern about this individual's dissipated habits and suggests he receives improper financial support, to which Mrs. Sparsit responds with sympathetic sighs and head shakes.
c15:p46: Bitzer informs Mrs. Sparsit at the Bank that a dissipated, extravagant individual (Thomas) who works there is to be pitied because his friend and relation at court supplies him with money, suggesting the funds come from Mr. Bounderby's pocket.
c15:p47: Mrs. Sparsit and Bitzer discuss an unnamed young man ("an individual") who is dissolute and improvident, relying on a patron for financial support. Mrs. Sparsit expresses her pity for the delusion that keeps this person dependent.
c15:p48: Bitzer, the light porter at the Bank, is reporting to Mrs. Sparsit about an unnamed individual (later revealed to be Tom Gradgrind) whom he suspects of being dissolute and improvident. Mrs. Sparsit has instructed him not to use names, so he refers obliquely to this person while criticizing their wasteful habits and lack of self-discipline, contrasting them with his own frugal and calculating nature.
c15:p49: Mrs. Sparsit encourages Bitzer, the bank's light porter and informant, to serve as a moral example to the working-class people of Coketown, praising his thrift and self-discipline as a model of proper conduct that the improvident factory workers should emulate.
c15:p50: Bitzer, the light porter and informer at the Bank, is responding to Mrs. Sparsit's suggestion that the working people of Coketown should follow his example of thrift and self-discipline. He boasts of his own financial prudence, claiming he saves his Christmas gratuity and lives below his wages, and argues that if he can achieve this, any worker should be able to do the same.
c15:p51: This passage appears in the narrative as an authorial commentary that interrupts Bitzer's conversation with Mrs. Sparsit. After Bitzer boasts about his personal thriftiness and claims "What one person can do, another can do," the narrator steps in to expose this as one of Coketown's prevalent myths—the false belief that workers can replicate the financial success of capitalists through individual effort alone, when in fact the system is rigged against them.
c15:p52: This passage is Bitzer's callous response to Mrs. Sparsit during their afternoon conversation at the Bank. He dismisses the workers' desires for leisure and argues that they could improve their circumstances through self-interest and mutual surveillance rather than collective action. The exchange demonstrates Bitzer's complete alignment with the utilitarian philosophy that dominates Coketown, his contempt for the working class, and his role as Mrs. Sparsit's informant on the town's affairs.
c15:p53: Mrs. Sparsit and Bitzer discuss the workers of Coketown. Bitzer suggests the workers pretend to want recreations and better living conditions, when they should focus on self-improvement through savings and labor, like he does. Mrs. Sparsit responds dismissively to his claim that workers merely pretend to want these things.
c15:p54: Bitzer, the Bank's spy and informer, argues to Mrs. Sparsit that workers are improvident and complaining. He uses himself as an example of someone who needs neither a wife, family, nor recreations to be content, questioning why workers should want or need these things when he doesn't.
c15:p55: Mrs. Sparsit and Bitzer discuss the poor working conditions and lack of ambition among Coketown's laborers. Bitzer argues that workers could improve their circumstances through prudence and self-denial, while Mrs. Sparsit agrees their improvidence is the root cause of their poverty and inability to provide for families.
c15:p56: Bitzer and Mrs. Sparsit discuss the improvidence of Coketown's working classes. Bitzer argues that workers are responsible for their own poverty due to lack of foresight, claiming that if they were more prudent they would prioritize feeding only themselves rather than supporting families they cannot afford.
c15:p57: Mrs. Sparsit sits at the Bank during afternoon tea, conversing with the light porter Bitzer about the working classes of Coketown. She agrees with Bitzer's argument that workers are improvident and would benefit from self-restraint and family planning if they were more prudent, while she eats muffin.
c15:p58: Mrs. Sparsit takes tea at the Bank in the late afternoon while conversing with Bitzer, the light porter and house spy. After a lengthy discussion about the improvidence of the working classes and their unions, Bitzer politely offers to fetch Mrs. Sparsit more refreshments, demonstrating his deferential manner toward her.
c15:p59: Mrs. Sparsit declines Bitzer's offer to fetch anything while she takes tea in the Bank's office after hours, as she observes a gentleman approaching the building who wishes to see her.
c15:p60: Bitzer informs Mrs. Sparsit of an unexpected visitor arriving at the Bank in the evening. This moment marks the introduction of a mysterious gentleman bearing a letter of introduction to Mr. Bounderby, which will lead to a significant conversation between Mrs. Sparsit and this stranger about Bounderby and his wife.
c15:p61: A stranger has arrived at the Bank seeking Mr. Bounderby's address. Bitzer, the light porter, informs Mrs. Sparsit that a gentleman is at the door and asks whether she wishes to see him.
c15:p62: A stranger has arrived at the Bank asking to speak with Mrs. Sparsit. Bitzer, the light porter, has informed her that a gentleman is at the door. Mrs. Sparsit, uncertain of the visitor's identity, wipes her mouth and arranges her mittens before agreeing to see him, maintaining her dignity as she fulfills her duties under Mr. Bounderby's authority.
c15:p63: Bitzer's brief reply to Mrs. Sparsit when she asks who the visitor at the Bank is, confirming that an unknown gentleman has arrived seeking Mr. Bounderby and requesting to see her.
c15:p64: A well-dressed stranger arrives at the Bank in the evening seeking Mr. Bounderby's address. Mrs. Sparsit, despite her puzzlement about his business at this late hour, decides to receive him out of her sense of duty and loyalty to her employer Mr. Bounderby, instructing Bitzer to use his judgment in showing the visitor in.
c15:p65: Mrs. Sparsit, who holds a position at the Bank in Coketown, receives an unexpected visitor in the evening. After a gentleman asks to see her and repeats his knock, she hastily hides her tea table and retreats upstairs to reappear with greater formality and dignity, as befits her sense of propriety and station.
c15:p66: A well-dressed stranger has arrived at the Bank asking for Mr. Bounderby's address. Mrs. Sparsit, having concealed her tea and prepared herself, now descends to meet this mysterious visitor in the board-room with great formality and dignity.
c15:p67: A well-dressed stranger arrives at the Bank seeking directions to Mr. Bounderby's residence, bearing a letter of introduction. Mrs. Sparsit receives him with formal dignity, and this passage describes his casual, world-weary demeanor as he stands at the window—indifferent to her impressive manner of entering, whistling coolly with his hat still on, presenting himself as a fashionable gentleman of refined exhaustion and cynical detachment.
c15:p68: Mrs. Sparsit, a widow working at Mr. Bounderby's Bank in the industrial town of Coketown, greets an unexpected visitor who has arrived at the Bank in the evening seeking directions to Mr. Bounderby's residence. This marks the introduction of a well-dressed gentleman bearing a letter of introduction from the politician Gradgrind.
c15:p69: A well-dressed stranger arrives at the Bank seeking directions to Mr. Bounderby's residence, carrying a letter of introduction. Upon meeting Mrs. Sparsit, he politely apologizes for his intrusion and removes his hat in greeting.
c15:p70: A well-dressed stranger arrives at the Bank seeking directions to Mr. Bounderby. Mrs. Sparsit makes a formal entrance to greet him, and in this moment of first meeting, she quickly assesses his appearance and demeanor with a keen, practiced eye.
c15:p71: Mrs. Sparsit receives an unexpected visitor at the Bank in the evening. A well-dressed gentleman arrives bearing a letter of introduction to Mr. Bounderby from the member of Parliament. After Bitzer announces him, Mrs. Sparsit composes herself and enters the board-room with dignity to greet this stranger, who requests information about where Mr. Bounderby resides.
c15:p72: A well-dressed gentleman caller arrives at the Bank seeking directions to Mr. Bounderby's residence. He has a letter of introduction from Gradgrind and, after observing Mrs. Sparsit at the window, enters the board-room to inquire about the banker's address. He now seats himself and begins conversing with Mrs. Sparsit, remarking on Coketown's black, industrial appearance.
c15:p73: A mysterious gentleman visitor arrives at the Bank seeking Mr. Bounderby's address. When he asks if Coketown is always as black as it appears, Mrs. Sparsit responds that it is generally much blacker, characterizing the town's perpetual industrial gloom.
c15:p74: A well-dressed stranger has arrived at the Bank with a letter of introduction to Mr. Bounderby. After Mrs. Sparsit provides directions to Bounderby's residence, the stranger engages her in conversation, commenting on Coketown's blackness and asking whether she is a native of the town.
c15:p75: Mrs. Sparsit, the Bank manager's assistant, is speaking with a well-dressed stranger who has arrived at the Bank seeking Mr. Bounderby's address. When the stranger asks if she is a native of Coketown, Mrs. Sparsit reveals her aristocratic past, explaining that she was once married to a man of the Powler family and moved in a superior social sphere before becoming a widow.
c15:p76: Mrs. Sparsit mentions that her late husband was a Powler, a distinguished family name. The stranger, a gentleman visitor bearing a letter of introduction to Mr. Bounderby, responds with surprise and curiosity upon hearing this reference to the Powler family, seeking confirmation of her connection to this notable lineage.
c15:p77: Mrs. Sparsit is explaining her background to a visiting gentleman who has come to the Bank seeking Mr. Bounderby's address. When he questions whether she is a native of Coketown, she mentions that her deceased husband was a Powler, a member of a prominent family. The gentleman seems unfamiliar with the name, prompting her to repeat it.
c15:p78: A well-dressed stranger arrives at the Bank bearing a letter of introduction to Mr. Bounderby. When Mrs. Sparsit mentions her late husband was a Powler, the stranger recognizes the family name, though the reference seems to exhaust rather than interest him.
c15:p79: The mysterious gentleman visitor, who has come to the Bank with a letter of introduction to Mr. Bounderby from Gradgrind, makes this remark to Mrs. Sparsit after she mentions her former life as a Powler before becoming a widow and settling in industrial Coketown.
c15:p80: Mrs. Sparsit explains her acceptance of her current position in Coketown to a well-dressed stranger who has just arrived at the Bank bearing a letter of introduction to Mr. Bounderby. When the stranger suggests she must be bored in this industrial town, she responds philosophically about her circumstances.
c15:p81: A well-dressed stranger bearing a letter of introduction to Mr. Bounderby arrives at the Bank and engages Mrs. Sparsit in conversation. When she describes herself as a servant of circumstances who has adapted to her governing power, the stranger responds with mild, dismissive indifference, playing with his watch-chain to show his weariness and lack of genuine interest in her philosophical sentiments.

c16:p0: This passage introduces the Gradgrind faction's recruitment strategy, explaining how they seek to enlist cynical, wealthy gentlemen—men who have rejected conventional values and morality—to advance their utilitarian political and economic agenda. It sets up the thematic conflict between the Gradgrind school's pursuit of hard facts and profit over human values (the "Graces"), and establishes why such morally indifferent men are attractive recruits for their cause. This opening paragraph frames the subsequent introduction of James Harthouse as an exemplary specimen of exactly this type of recruit.
c16:p1: This passage appears in the opening of the chapter as part of Dickens's satirical commentary on the Gradgrind school's adoption of the cynical attitudes of wealthy dandies and "fine gentlemen." It describes how the Gradgrind educators, despite publicly pretending to disdain gentlemanly affectation, actually imitate and are attracted to the idle sophistication of these upper-class figures, resulting in a degraded hybrid of false politeness and mechanical instruction in utilitarian political economy. The passage sets up the ideological corruption that will be embodied in the character James Harthouse, the fashionable gentleman who is about to be introduced into Coketown.
c16:p2: This chunk introduces James Harthouse, a charming but cynical gentleman from a good family who has gained political prominence through his wit and rhetorical skill. The passage exemplifies his character through a specific anecdote: his ability to trivialize a serious railway disaster that killed five people and wounded thirty-two by making a joke of it before Parliament—placing a widow's cap on a dead cow to entertain the House of Commons. This introduction establishes Harthouse as morally corrupt and superficial, setting up his later arrival in Coketown where he will become a destructive influence on the Bounderby household.
c16:p3: This passage introduces James Harthouse, a bored gentleman of good family who has failed at various pursuits (military service, diplomatic work, travel) and is now being sent to Coketown to enter politics and statistics under Mr. Gradgrind's patronage. His older brother, an MP, recommends him as a talented speaker, and the passage explains how Harthouse comes to arrive in Coketown with a letter of introduction to Mr. Bounderby.
c16:p4: Mr. Bounderby has received a letter of introduction from Mr. Gradgrind recommending James Harthouse, a bored gentleman seeking entry into politics and statistics. Bounderby immediately visits Harthouse at his hotel to make his acquaintance and warn him about Coketown before introducing him to society.
c16:p5: Bounderby arrives at the hotel to meet James Harthouse, a new political recruit sent by Gradgrind. Bounderby introduces himself and begins to tell Harthouse about Coketown and its industrial values.

c16:p10: Mr. Bounderby meets James Harthouse at his hotel and begins explaining Coketown's values to him—its industrial prosperity, the pleasantness of mill work, and workers' supposed desires for luxury. c16:p11: Bounderby introduces James Harthouse to Coketown by making false claims about the superior conditions of mill work, asserting that the mills are already perfect and the workers are well-paid, while dismissing any criticism or need for improvement.
c16:p12: James Harthouse arrives in Coketown and meets Mr. Bounderby, who explains his views on the town's mills and workers. c16:p13: Bounderby is introducing James Harthouse to Coketown by describing the town's industrial character and dismissing workers' aspirations. c16:p14: James Harthouse has just arrived in Coketown and Mr. Bounderby is introducing him to the town by explaining his views on industrial work, the mills, and the working class. c16:p15: Bounderby meets James Harthouse at his hotel and establishes their acquaintance by declaring his working-class origins and dismissing any pretense to gentility, asserting his pride in his self-made status despite his humble beginnings.

c16:p26: James Harthouse, newly introduced to Coketown and the Bounderby household, makes a flattering comment about Mr. Bounderby to Louisa during their first meeting in the drawing-room, characterizing Bounderby as refreshingly natural compared to his own conventional manner.

c16:p28: James Harthouse is momentarily flustered when Louisa Bounderby responds coolly to his compliment about her brother, unsettling him with her reserved manner and indirect wit.
c16:p29: James Harthouse has just arrived in Coketown as a young gentleman seeking political advancement through Mr. Gradgrind's patronage. c16:p32: James Harthouse reveals his cynical philosophy to Louisa Bounderby during their first meeting at the Bounderby household. c16:p33: James Harthouse, a cynical political recruit sent to Coketown by Mr. Gradgrind, meets Louisa Bounderby for the first time at her home. c16:p34: Louisa responds to James Harthouse's cynical admission that he has no genuine political beliefs and will support whatever ideas seem expedient, comparing them to a mathematical system. She calls out his opportunistic approach to politics.
c16:p35: James Harthouse remarks cynically to Louisa Bounderby that those who lack genuine convictions or beliefs—like himself—form a vast, unnamed political faction. c16:p36:
# Context: Harthouse's First Day in Coketown

James Harthouse, a bored gentleman newly introduced to Coketown politics, has just met Mr. Bounderby and his wife Louisa at their home. During conversation, Louisa engages Harthouse in witty political discussion, causing Bounderby to grow impatient. To interrupt their exchange, Bounderby proposes taking Harthouse on a tour of local notables before dinner, successfully redirecting attention away from the intellectual sparring between Louisa and his guest.
c16:p37: Mr. Bounderby entertains James Harthouse at dinner, recounting exaggerated anecdotes of his impoverished youth—eating stewed eels and drinking inferior water as a child, consuming horses disguised as processed meats. Harthouse responds politely but with indifference, remaining more interested in observing Louisa Bounderby than in Bounderby's self-aggrandizing stories.
c16:p38: James Harthouse, newly introduced to Coketown society, dines with Mr. and Mrs. Bounderby. Observing Louisa Bounderby's impassive demeanor throughout the meal, he wonders if anything can provoke an emotional response from her seemingly unmoved face.
c16:p39: Louisa Bounderby sits impassively at the dinner table, unmoved by conversation, until her brother Tom arrives late. Her face transforms with genuine emotion—the only person who can elicit a real emotional response from her constrained and reserved demeanor.
c16:p40: Tom arrives late to dinner. Louisa, who has been impassive and emotionless throughout James Harthouse's visit, suddenly smiles radiantly and reaches for her brother's hand with evident affection, revealing that Tom is the only person she truly cares for. This moment reveals a crack in her cold exterior and captures Harthouse's attention as a potential weakness to exploit.
c16:p41: James Harthouse observes Louisa's sudden emotional transformation when her brother Tom enters the dining room, noting her genuine smile and affection toward him—the only person who seems to move her constrained, emotionally guarded demeanor. This observation becomes pivotal to Harthouse's strategy of seduction, as he recognizes Tom as Louisa's sole emotional attachment and potential leverage to gain influence over her.
c16:p42: Tom Gradgrind arrives late to dinner at his brother-in-law Bounderby's house, where the new acquaintance James Harthouse is being entertained. Bounderby scolds Tom for his tardiness, and Tom defensively responds about his work obligations. Harthouse then engages Tom in conversation, beginning to cultivate a manipulative friendship with him.
c16:p43: Bounderby rebukes Tom Gradgrind for arriving late to dinner, comparing his own youthful discipline to Tom's tardiness. This occurs during the dinner scene where James Harthouse is a guest at the Bounderby household, and marks the beginning of Tom's interactions with Harthouse, who will later become a corrupting influence on the young man.
c16:p44: Tom defends his late arrival at dinner by contrasting his current responsibilities at the bank with Bounderby's situation at the same age, implying that Bounderby had fewer obligations.
c16:p45: At the dinner table, Tom arrives late. Bounderby criticizes his punctuality, comparing it to his own strict discipline in youth. c16:p46: Tom responds defensively to Bounderby's criticism about his unpunctuality at dinner, refusing to accept a lecture from his employer and brother-in-law.
c16:p47: James Harthouse has been introduced to Mr. Bounderby's household and is dining with the family. During dinner, Tom arrives late and engages in a tense exchange with Bounderby. c16:p48: Louisa Bounderby responds to James Harthouse's question about whether he has seen her brother Tom abroad, clarifying that Tom was educated at home and has never traveled abroad. c16:p49: Tom Gradgrind responds to James Harthouse's question about whether he has seen Tom abroad or at school. Tom denies having traveled abroad and confirms he was educated at home, prompting his curt reply that he has had "no such luck" in having traveled.
c16:p50: James Harthouse observes Tom Gradgrind's ungracious behavior toward his sister Louisa at dinner, and recognizes that despite Tom's sullenness, Louisa's affection for him reveals her emotional isolation and desperate need for connection, making Tom the only person she genuinely cares for.
c16:p51: James Harthouse, a fashionable but aimless gentleman newly arrived in Coketown as a political candidate, is introduced to the Bounderby household. c16:p52: This passage appears in paragraph [P52], serving as a critical authorial commentary on Tom Gradgrind's character. The chunk explains the psychological origins of Tom's hypocrisy and moral weakness—the result of Mr. Gradgrind's system of rigid factual education that has suppressed his natural imagination and left him vulnerable to base impulses. This commentary provides key insight into how Gradgrind's utilitarian educational philosophy has corrupted his son, setting up Tom's susceptibility to Harthouse's manipulative influence.
c16:p53: James Harthouse, a newly arrived politician from London, has spent the evening at the Bounderby household and is now walking back to his hotel with Tom Gradgrind (Louisa's brother). c16:p54: James Harthouse asks Tom if he smokes upon arriving at his hotel room. Tom enthusiastically responds with "I believe you!" expressing his eager willingness to smoke with his new acquaintance, whom he is quickly coming to admire.
c16:p55: James Harthouse invites young Tom Gradgrind back to his hotel room after escorting him there. c16:p56: Tom observes James Harthouse's casual elegance and effortless style while they smoke together in Harthouse's hotel room after dinner. Tom is impressed by Harthouse's apparent indifference to appearance combined with his refined presentation.
c16:p57: James Harthouse invites Tom to his hotel room after dinner, where he offers him tobacco and drinks. Noticing Tom hasn't been drinking, Harthouse refills his glass, beginning to manipulate the young man through hospitality and flattery.
c16:p58: Tom Gradgrind, after dinner at his sister Louisa's house, accompanies the newly arrived James Harthouse back to his hotel. Once there, Harthouse invites Tom inside for drinks and cigars. c16:p59: Tom is testing Mr. Harthouse's true opinion of Mr. Bounderby by making disparaging remarks about him. c16:p60: Tom mockingly agrees with Harthouse's flattering comment about Bounderby, closing one eye in a conspiratorial gesture that signals his contempt for his brother-in-law beneath the surface politeness of their conversation.
c16:p61: James Harthouse, having established rapport with the bored young Tom Bounderby through drinks and tobacco at his hotel, adopts a deliberately seductive and manipulative posture—physically dominating and psychologically penetrating—as he begins to test Tom's loyalty to his family and draw out his resentments.
c16:p62: James Harthouse, a charming gentleman newly introduced to Coketown, encounters Tom Gradgrind at Mr. Bounderby's dinner table. c16:p64: James Harthouse, a cynical and bored gentleman newly arrived in Coketown to pursue politics, has been entertaining Tom Gradgrind at his hotel room with tobacco and drinks. c16:p65: James Harthouse, a charming but cynical gentleman, has been introduced to Coketown and the Bounderby household. After dinner, he invites Tom (Louisa's brother) to his hotel room. c16:p66: Tom Gradgrind, emboldened by James Harthouse's casual intimacy and flattery, openly expresses his contempt for his brother-in-law Mr. Bounderby during a late-night visit to Harthouse's hotel room. c16:p67: James Harthouse warns Tom to be discreet about his contemptuous remarks regarding Mr. Bounderby when Louisa (Tom's sister and Bounderby's wife) is present, during their private conversation at Harthouse's hotel room after dinner.
c16:p68: Tom responds dismissively to James Harthouse's warning to be careful around his sister Louisa when speaking disrespectfully of Mr. Bounderby. Tom's flippant reaction reveals his lack of regard for his sister's feelings and his growing comfort with Harthouse's company.
c16:p69: James Harthouse, a cynical political operative newly arrived in Coketown, has invited Tom Bounderby (the "whelp") back to his hotel room after dinner.
