c19:p72: Tom Harthouse whispers urgently to Stephen Blackpool on the stairs, offering to help him and giving cryptic instructions to wait near the Bank. The vivid description of his heated breath conveys Tom's intense, agitated manner as he speaks.
c19:p73: Tom Harthouse reveals to Stephen Blackpool that the Bank messenger who delivered Bounderby's summons is a light porter at the Bank where Tom himself works, setting up a mysterious scheme to help Stephen before he leaves Coketown.
c19:p74: Tom Gradgrind hurriedly takes Stephen Blackpool outside on the stairs after Louisa's visit to Stephen's lodgings. Tom whispers that he may be able to help Stephen find work, speaking in a rushed and confused manner, which causes Stephen to internally note Tom's agitation.
c19:p75: Tom Gradgrind is asking Stephen Blackpool when he plans to leave Coketown. This occurs during Tom's private conversation with Stephen on the stairs, after Tom has hinted that he may be able to help Stephen find new employment at the Bank, where Tom himself works.
c19:p76: Stephen tells Tom Hardin that he plans to leave Coketown on Friday or Saturday, after being rejected by his employer and forced to seek work elsewhere due to his refusal to join the workers' union.
c19:p77: Tom Gradgrind pulls Stephen Blackpool aside on the stairs after Louisa's visit to Stephen's room. Tom cryptically offers to help Stephen, hinting at a plan involving the Bank's light porter, without revealing what it is. He instructs Stephen to loiter near the Bank in the coming days to await a message.
c19:p78: Tom is asking Stephen if he recognizes the light porter from the Bank, and Stephen confirms that he does know him and will be able to identify him again.
c19:p79: Tom Harthouse instructs Stephen Blackpool to loiter near the Bank in the evenings before his departure from Coketown, promising a potential message or note if he can arrange a service to help Stephen. Tom warns Stephen to act casually and not draw attention, emphasizing the conditional nature of his assistance.
c19:p80: Tom Gradgrind pulls Stephen Blackpool aside on the dark stairs after his sister Louisa's visit to Stephen's room. Tom whispers that he may be able to help Stephen find employment, instructing him to loiter near the Bank over the next few days where a light porter may deliver a message. While giving these cryptic instructions in the darkness, Tom grabs and twists Stephen's coat in an agitated, peculiar manner.
c19:p81: Stephen agrees to Tom Harthouse's cryptic plan to help him find work by waiting outside the Bank at night for a message from the light porter, without asking questions about the arrangement.
c19:p82: Tom Harthouse urges Stephen Blackpool to loiter near the Bank on the evenings before his departure, promising a possible "good turn" through the light porter. Tom repeatedly emphasizes the need for secrecy and Stephen's understanding of the arrangement, claiming he will inform his sister Louisa of the plan and assuring Stephen all will be well if he simply waits as instructed.
c19:p83: Tom Gradgrind rushes Stephen Blackpool out of his lodgings after speaking to him privately about a mysterious scheme to help him, then departs hastily with his sister Louisa without waiting for her to descend the stairs properly.
c19:p84: After Louisa Bounderby visits Stephen's lodgings to offer him financial assistance for his departure from Coketown, and her brother Tom gives Stephen cryptic instructions to wait by the Bank, Mrs. Pegler emerges from her hiding place. Despite her earlier agitation at Bounderby's name, she has developed an admiration for Louisa. The group then disbands, with Stephen and Rachael accompanying Mrs. Pegler to her lodgings at the Travellers' Coffee House before parting ways.
c19:p85: Stephen Blackpool prepares to leave Coketown after being ostracized by his employer and fellow workers. After a visit from Mrs. Bounderby (Louisa) and her brother Tom, Stephen escorts the mysterious Mrs. Pegler to her lodging. He and Rachael then walk back together in silence, approaching the corner where they must part ways, their relationship constrained by Stephen's earlier promise to her.
c19:p86: Stephen is saying goodbye to Rachael after walking her home from escorting Mrs. Pegler to her lodgings. He is preparing to leave Coketown the next morning after losing his job at the mill and being ostracized by both workers and employers. This moment captures their final parting, where Stephen expresses his hope to see her once more before his departure, though he acknowledges the likelihood that their "old agreement" to avoid being seen together will prevent it.
c19:p87: Stephen and Rachael are parting ways at a street corner after an unexpected visit from Louisa Bounderby to Stephen's lodgings. Stephen has decided to leave Coketown because his association with a union promise has made him unemployable. Rachael is acknowledging that they must accept they will likely not see each other again before his departure, and they should be honest about this painful separation.
c19:p88: Stephen tells Rachael that to protect her reputation, they should not be seen together in the remaining days before he leaves Coketown, as association with him—now shunned as a troublemaker—could bring her unwanted trouble.
c19:p89: Stephen and Rachael discuss their parting before he leaves Coketown. Rachael refuses to avoid being seen with Stephen despite potential trouble, clarifying that their separation is required by the promise he made to her not to join the trade union—their "old agreement"—not out of fear for herself.
c19:p90: Stephen agrees with Rachael that they should not be seen together before his departure from Coketown, as it could bring her into trouble, despite their deep mutual affection.
c19:p91: Stephen and Rachael part ways at a dark street corner after Mrs. Pegler leaves. As they prepare to separate, knowing Stephen must leave Coketown, Rachael asks if he will write to her about his future travels.
c19:p92: Stephen Blackpool bids farewell to Rachael at the dark corner where they always meet, expressing his gratitude and blessing her as they part, knowing he must leave Coketown to start anew after being cast out by his employer and shunned by his fellow workers.
c19:p93: This is Rachael's blessing to Stephen as they part ways at night on a street corner. Stephen is leaving Coketown after being ostracized by his fellow workers and rejected by his employer Mr. Bounderby. Rachael, the woman he loves but cannot be with due to their promise to remain apart, offers this final benediction before they must separate, knowing they will not see each other again before his departure.
c19:p94: Stephen Blackpool says farewell to Rachael after an emotional parting at the dark corner of her street. This is their final conversation before Stephen leaves Coketown, as he has been forced to quit his job and seek work elsewhere due to his refusal to join the union and the social ostracism that followed. Rachael has been his moral compass throughout his troubles, and in this goodbye, Stephen expresses his deep gratitude for how her goodness has helped him see his suffering with greater dignity.
c19:p95: Stephen Blackpool and Rachael part ways at a dark street corner after an emotional evening. Stephen is leaving Coketown the next morning, having lost his job and been rejected by both his employer and fellow workers. Their farewell, though brief and in an ordinary street, carries deep significance as a sacred moment between two working-class people bound by love and principle. The narrator then delivers a critical commentary on utilitarian philosophy and its dehumanizing effects on the poor, warning that stripping romance and emotional grace from the working classes will ultimately lead to social catastrophe.
c19:p96: Stephen, having left his employment with Mr. Bounderby and promised to depart Coketown, works his final days while socially ostracized by his fellow workers. He prepares to leave town to seek employment elsewhere, continuing to await a potential message from Tom Harthouse at the Bank before his departure.
c19:p97: Stephen keeps watch outside the Bank as Tom Harthouse instructed, hoping for a message that might help him before leaving Coketown. On the third and final evening, he resolves to wait longer, though nothing has occurred on the previous two nights.
c19:p98: Stephen waits outside the Bank for two hours on his final evening in Coketown, hoping to receive a message from Tom Harmon about a potential job opportunity. While lingering outside, he observes Mrs. Sparsit at the first-floor window and the light porter, but no communication is made to him.
c19:p99: Stephen waits outside the Bank for two hours on his last evening in Coketown, following Tom's cryptic instructions to expect a possible message or note. During this lonely vigil, he anxiously loiters in the street, feeling self-conscious and disreputable as he watches for any sign from Tom's contact, the light porter.
c19:p100: Stephen waits outside the Bank for two hours, as Tom Gradgrind instructed him, hoping to receive a message that might help him leave Coketown. As evening falls and the lamplighter arrives, Mrs. Sparsit and the light porter move through the Bank's windows, but no message comes. Stephen, relieved that his vigil is over, departs quickly.
c19:p101: Stephen Blackpool prepares to leave Coketown after losing his job and being ostracized by both workers and employers. Having said farewell to Rachael and completed his final days of work, he makes arrangements for an early departure the next morning before the factory workers emerge into the streets.
c19:p102: Stephen Blackpool leaves Coketown early in the morning after being rejected by his employer Mr. Bounderby and shunned by his fellow workers. He departs the town as an outcast, carrying his bundle and looking back at the place he must abandon to seek work elsewhere.
c19:p103: Stephen Blackpool leaves Coketown early in the morning after being forced to resign from his job due to his refusal to join the union. As he departs the industrial town, he passes by landmarks including Rachael's home, factories, and the railway, taking a final look back at Coketown from the hilltop before beginning his journey to seek work elsewhere.
c19:p104: Stephen Blackpool leaves Coketown at dawn after being forced to quit his job and part from Rachael. As he reaches the top of a hill and looks back at the town, he observes the early morning light breaking over the industrial landscape of factories and chimneys, which obscure the sun with their smoke.
c19:p105: Stephen Blackpool departs Coketown after losing his job and being ostracized by both workers and employers. Having said farewell to Rachael, his beloved, he leaves town at daybreak, reflecting on the strange transition from industrial life to the open road ahead.
c2:p0: **Context:** This is the opening passage of Chapter 1, introducing Thomas Gradgrind, the protagonist and central figure of the novel. It presents his character through a third-person narrative that mimics his own self-introduction, establishing him as a man obsessed with facts, calculations, and rigid rationality. The passage emphasizes his rejection of imagination, emotion, and anything that cannot be measured or quantified—themes that will dominate the chapter as he teaches in a schoolroom and attempts to suppress his students' capacity for fancy and imagination.
c2:p1: This chunk comes at the beginning of the chapter, right after Gradgrind's self-introduction, showing how he applies his rigid, fact-based philosophy to teaching schoolchildren. It marks the transition from his abstract principles to their practical application in the classroom, establishing his method of presenting himself and his educational ideology to his students.
c2:p2: This passage describes Thomas Gradgrind's appearance and demeanor as he stands before a classroom of students, comparing him to mechanical devices that will forcefully eliminate imagination and replace it with facts. It illustrates the novel's central conflict between rigid factual education and imaginative thinking, occurring as Gradgrind prepares to teach his pupils through systematic, emotionless instruction.
c2:p3: Mr. Gradgrind, a strict educator obsessed with facts and figures, begins questioning students in his classroom. He singles out a girl he doesn't recognize, initiating an exchange that reveals her name is Sissy Jupe and her father works in horse-riding—a background Gradgrind disapproves of as lacking in factual utility.
c2:p4: Mr. Gradgrind demands that "Girl number twenty" identify herself. She responds with her name, Sissy Jupe, while nervously demonstrating the deference expected in his strict, fact-based classroom.
c2:p5: Mr. Gradgrind interrogates a young girl from a circus family about her name and background, dismissing her informal nickname "Sissy" and insisting she adopt the more formal name "Cecilia" as part of his rigid fact-based educational philosophy.
c2:p6: Sissy Jupe, a student in Mr. Gradgrind's classroom, defends her informal name against his insistence that she call herself by her proper name, Cecilia, revealing her affection for her father despite Gradgrind's disapproval of his circus background.
c2:p7: Mr. Gradgrind corrects Sissy Jupe for using the informal nickname "Sissy" instead of her proper name "Cecilia," then interrogates her about her father's occupation.
c2:p8: Sissy Jupe's response when Mr. Gradgrind asks her father's occupation during a classroom examination, revealing her background in the circus rather than respectable industrial society.
c2:p9: Mr. Gradgrind dismisses Sissy Jupe's father's occupation in the circus. When Sissy explains that her father works in horse-riding, Gradgrind reacts with disapproval, frowning and gesturing dismissively because he considers the circus an unsuitable and unFactual profession beneath serious discussion in his school of hard facts.
c2:p10: Mr. Gradgrind interrogates Sissy Jupe about her father's occupation, dismissing her reference to circus horse-riding as irrelevant to his fact-based education system. He insists on reducing her father's work to the utilitarian term "horsebreaker" rather than acknowledging the circus context.
c2:p11: Sissy Jupe's response to Mr. Gradgrind's questioning about her father's occupation. When Gradgrind dismisses her mention of "horse-riding" and the circus ring, Sissy explains that her father breaks horses in the ring when work is available, emphasizing the circus/performance context that Gradgrind finds objectionable.
c2:p12: In this scene, Mr. Gradgrind interrogates Sissy Jupe about her father's occupation. He dismisses her mention of the circus ring where her father performs horse-riding and attempts to redefine his work in purely factual, utilitarian terms—as a horsebreaker and veterinary surgeon—rather than acknowledging the imaginative world of performance from which she comes.
c2:p13: Sissy Jupe confirms that her father, who breaks horses, also treats sick animals when questioned by Mr. Gradgrind during a classroom examination about occupations and facts.
c2:p14: Mr. Gradgrind interrogates Sissy Jupe about her father's occupation, dismissing his work in horse-riding as irrelevant. After learning her father breaks and doctors horses, Gradgrind demands she provide a factual definition of a horse, testing her knowledge of facts.
c2:p15: Sissy Jupe is unable to answer Mr. Gradgrind's demand that she define a horse, which embarrasses and alarms her. This moment contrasts her imaginative nature with the utilitarian, fact-based education system being imposed in the schoolroom.
c2:p16: This chunk occurs during Mr. Gradgrind's classroom examination where he tests students on their factual knowledge. After questioning Sissy Jupe about her father's occupation in the circus, Gradgrind demands she define a horse. When Sissy cannot provide a definition, he publicly shames her and calls on Bitzer, a pale, emotionless boy, to demonstrate the "correct" factual definition of a horse as a mere collection of anatomical and biological facts.
c2:p17: Mr. Gradgrind calls upon "Girl number twenty" (Sissy Jupe) to define a horse. When she cannot answer, he turns to another student, Bitzer, who provides a detailed, factual definition. This passage describes the physical contrast between Sissy and Bitzer as Mr. Gradgrind selects Bitzer to answer, illustrating the opposition between Sissy's imagination and Bitzer's mechanical, fact-based nature.
c2:p18: In a schoolroom, Mr. Gradgrind calls on a student named Bitzer to provide a factual definition of a horse after the girl Sissy Jupe has failed to answer the question. Bitzer responds with a technical, scientific definition emphasizing facts and figures, exemplifying the educational philosophy that dominates the lesson.
c2:p19: This is Bitzer's textbook definition of a horse, given as the "correct" answer to Mr. Gradgrind's demand that student Sissy Jupe define a horse. It exemplifies the mechanical, fact-based education system that prioritizes rote memorization of scientific and technical details over imagination and personal experience.
c2:p20: This occurs after Bitzer has provided a detailed, factual definition of a horse to Mr. Gradgrind's satisfaction, contrasting with Sissy Jupe's inability to define one. Gradgrind uses this moment to demonstrate to Sissy that she now understands what a horse is through Bitzer's recitation of facts and figures.
c2:p21: Sissy Jupe is humiliated after failing to define a horse, while Bitzer successfully recites a detailed factual definition. Mr. Gradgrind and the gentleman examiner praise Bitzer's purely factual approach, demonstrating the novel's critique of mechanistic education that privileges facts over imagination and feeling.
c2:p22: This passage introduces a third gentleman—a government official—who arrives at Mr. Gradgrind's school to conduct an examination of the students. Using boxing metaphors, Dickens satirically describes him as a combative bureaucrat tasked with enforcing the principle of "Fact" over imagination, setting up his interrogation of the children about whether they would decorate rooms with representations of horses.
c2:p23: A government official questions students about aesthetic principles, asking whether one should decorate a room with pictures of horses, beginning to establish his philosophy that decoration should strictly mirror reality.
c2:p24: The government official conducting a lesson on taste and fact asks the schoolchildren whether they would paper a room with representations of horses. The children, conditioned to follow the gentleman's cues rather than think independently, respond in divided chorus—first half saying "Yes," then switching to "No" upon seeing his disapproving expression, illustrating the mechanical, unthinking nature of their education.
c2:p25: A government official questions students about whether they would paper a room with representations of horses. After the children give conflicting answers, the official dismisses their "yes" responses and begins explaining the principle that one should only use in decoration what exists in reality.
c2:p26: A government official is testing schoolchildren on practical reasoning by asking whether they would paper a room with representations of horses. When he demands they must paper it, one slow boy suggests an alternative: painting the room instead, which the official rejects as incorrect thinking based on fact.
c2:p27: The gentleman questioning the children about whether they would paper a room with horse representations becomes impatient when a boy suggests he would paint it instead of papering it. The gentleman insists the room must be papered, correcting the boy's objection by emphasizing that decoration must strictly adhere to facts and reality, not imagination or personal preference.
c2:p28: A government official is conducting a lesson on "Taste" by questioning students about whether they would use decorative items in their homes. When a boy suggests he would paint a room instead of papering it, Gradgrind sternly insists that the boy must accept the premise of papering the room, dismissing his alternative idea as irrelevant to the lesson's focus on facts and reality.
c2:p29: The government officer is explaining to the students why they should not use decorative patterns with horses on wallpaper, using the principle that design should only depict what exists in reality. This is part of his lesson on the doctrine that "Taste is only another name for Fact," rejecting imagination and fancy in favor of strict adherence to factual reality.
c2:p30: The children in Mr. Gradgrind's classroom are being examined by a government official on questions of fact and reason. When asked whether they would paper a room with representations of horses, the children automatically divide into two groups giving opposite answers, demonstrating their conditioned response to conform to what they perceive as the "correct" fact-based answer rather than thinking independently.
c2:p31: This passage occurs during a lesson where a government official is teaching schoolchildren about practical reasoning and facts. He has just asked whether they would paper a room with representations of horses, leading them to realize that since horses don't walk on walls in reality, they shouldn't depict them on wallpaper. Here, he articulates the core principle of the utilitarian education system: that taste and aesthetics must be governed entirely by factual reality, with no allowance for imagination or fancy. Thomas Gradgrind approves of this doctrine.
c2:p32: The gentleman inspector is establishing his utilitarian principle that people should only surround themselves with representations of things that exist in reality. He has just explained why you cannot paper a room with pictures of horses (since horses don't walk up and down real walls), and now tests this doctrine further by asking the children whether they would use a carpet with flower representations.
c2:p33: The government official conducting an examination of schoolchildren asks whether they would carpet a room with representations of flowers. Most children, having learned to give factual answers, chorus "No, sir!" in agreement with utilitarian logic. Only a few children, including Sissy Jupe, answer "Yes," revealing her inclination toward imagination and beauty over strict fact-based reasoning.
c2:p34: The gentleman (a government official) has just challenged the students with a question about carpeting a room with flower representations. Sissy Jupe (Girl number twenty) is the only one who answers "Yes," going against the expected "No" answer. The gentleman now responds to her unconventional answer with calm condescension, preparing to lecture her about the superiority of fact over fancy.
c2:p35: Sissy Jupe is called out by the visiting gentleman for answering that she would carpet a room with representations of flowers, which contradicts the principle that one should only have what exists in fact. She stands up to respond to his questioning about her preference for flowers.
c2:p36: The government gentleman is examining Sissy Jupe on the principle that decoration and taste should be based solely on fact, not fancy. He questions why she would put flower representations on a carpet, challenging her preference for ornamental beauty over utilitarian reality.
c2:p37: Sissy Jupe responds to the gentleman's question about whether she would put flower representations on a carpet, defending her preference for fancy and beauty over strict factual reasoning, which contradicts the educational philosophy of facts being imposed in the classroom.
c2:p38: The government official questions Sissy Jupe about her desire to carpet a room with floral representations, challenging the practicality and logic of her aesthetic preference against the principle that taste should be based only on facts and reality.
c2:p39: Sissy Jupe argues for the aesthetic and imaginative value of flower-patterned carpets, defending her preference for beauty and fancy against the gentleman's strict adherence to factual reasoning.
c2:p40: Sissy Jupe, a student from a circus family, argues that she would carpet a room with flower representations because she loves flowers. The government gentleman interrupts her to emphasize that imagination and fancy must be completely suppressed in favor of strict adherence to fact and reality—a core principle of the utilitarian education system being imposed on the students.
c2:p41: Thomas Gradgrind and a government official are conducting an examination of schoolchildren, emphasizing that imagination and fancy must be entirely suppressed in favor of facts. After Sissy Jupe expresses her fondness for flowers and her desire to have floral representations on carpets, the official rebukes her for "fancying." Gradgrind then solemnly reinforces this reprimand, instructing Sissy that she must not indulge in any such imaginative thinking, as all aspects of life must be governed strictly by fact.
c2:p42: The gentleman and Thomas Gradgrind emphatically reinforce their doctrine that education and life must be governed entirely by facts, rejecting imagination and fancy. This occurs during their interrogation of Sissy Jupe, who has just admitted to wanting decorative flowers on a carpet because she finds them pretty—a response that violates their strict factual principles.
c2:p43: This is the gentleman examiner's climactic speech to the schoolchildren, explaining the strict utilitarian principle that all design and decoration must be based solely on observable fact, rejecting imagination and fancy. He uses examples of carpets with flowers and painted crockery to argue that representations must not contradict what exists in reality, and advocates for purely mathematical and geometric designs instead.
c2:p44: After being told by the government official that she must not use her imagination or "fancy" in any aspect of life—including refusing to put flower patterns on carpets because flowers don't actually walk on floors in reality—Sissy Jupe sits down, visibly shaken by the harsh, fact-based world these educators are forcing upon her.
c2:p45: The government gentleman proposes that Mr. M'Choakumchild, a newly trained schoolmaster, begin his first lesson while the gentleman observes his teaching methods, after having just completed an examination of the students on the definition of a horse and the principles of fact-based education.
c2:p46: Mr. Gradgrind agrees to allow the new schoolmaster M'Choakumchild to begin his first lesson after the government official finishes his examination of the students on facts and rejects imagination.
c2:p47: Mr. M'Choakumchild, the new schoolmaster, is introduced as he begins his first lesson. Dickens satirizes his mechanical, fact-based education through an extended description of his exhaustive but ultimately counterproductive training—he has been crammed with vast quantities of factual knowledge across numerous subjects, yet this overload of information ironically undermines his ability to teach effectively, reflecting the chapter's critique of utilitarian education that prioritizes facts over imagination and understanding.
c2:p48: This passage concludes the opening chapter of Hard Times, serving as the narrator's ironic commentary on Mr. M'Choakumchild, the newly trained schoolmaster who embodies the rigid fact-based educational philosophy advocated by Thomas Gradgrind and the government inspector. The narrator questions whether the relentless instruction in facts will completely destroy imaginative thinking (Fancy) in students like Sissy Jupe, or merely damage it. The Morgiana reference alludes to the tale from Arabian Nights, comparing the teacher's methodical examination of students' minds to Morgiana identifying thieves by pouring boiling oil into jars—a dark metaphor for the systematic destruction of childhood imagination through mechanical instruction.
c20:p0: This passage introduces James Harthouse as a politically ambitious but morally empty character who gains prominence through calculated dishonesty and studied indifference. It establishes his central trait of opportunistic cynicism—his ability to adopt any position without genuine conviction—which makes him an ideal corrupter of Louisa Bounderby and her brother Tom. The description sets up his later manipulations of both siblings and foreshadows the moral danger he represents to the Gradgrind household.
c20:p1: James Harthouse expresses his cynical philosophy to Mrs. Bounderby (Louisa), arguing that he and others like him are honest about society's hypocrisy by openly acknowledging that virtue and benevolence are meaningless, whereas hypocrites pretend to believe in these values while knowing they are false.
c20:p2: This chunk appears in the narrative reflection on Louisa's vulnerability to Harthouse's cynical philosophy. It follows Harthouse's declaration to Mrs. Bounderby that virtue and benevolence are meaningless pretenses, and precedes the narrator's analysis of how Louisa's soul has been hollowed by her father Gradgrind's utilitarian education, leaving her susceptible to Harthouse's nihilism. The passage emphasizes how Gradgrind's fact-based upbringing has already destroyed in Louisa what moral foundation might have protected her from seduction by Harthouse's worldly corruption.
c20:p3: This passage describes Louisa Bounderby's internal conflict as she encounters James Harthouse's cynical philosophy. It explains how her suppressed childhood longing for something beyond her father's rigid utilitarian education makes her vulnerable to Harthouse's nihilistic worldview, which offers her a false justification for her emotional emptiness and sacrifices, particularly her loveless marriage to Bounderby.
c20:p4: This passage describes the early stages of Mr. Harthouse's pursuit of Louisa Bounderby. It establishes his lazy, amoral character—lacking genuine wickedness or purpose, merely drifting into seduction through indifference. The text explains how Harthouse initially found Louisa striking and began frequenting the Bounderby household, encouraged by Mr. Bounderby's boastful welcome of his socially-connected visitor.
c20:p5: James Harthouse observes Louisa's animated expression when she hears her brother Tom mentioned, and becomes intrigued by the possibility of inspiring a similar emotional response in her himself, viewing her as a new conquest to pursue.
c20:p6: James Harthouse, a cynical gentleman newly arrived in Coketown, has begun cultivating a relationship with Louisa Bounderby by gaining her confidence through discussion of her brother Tom's financial troubles. This passage describes how Harthouse systematically studies Louisa's character by piecing together information Tom has revealed to him with his own careful observations of her behavior, beginning to manipulate her emotional vulnerabilities for his own amusement.
c20:p7: This passage describes Mr. Bounderby's country estate, located fifteen miles from Coketown and accessible by railway. It details the landscape's transition from industrial coal-mining terrain to pastoral countryside, and explains how Bounderby acquired the property through a bank foreclosure on a speculating magnate's mortgage—establishing the setting for subsequent scenes between Louisa, James Harthouse, and Tom at the house.
c20:p8: This passage describes Mr. Bounderby's behavior after acquiring a country estate near Coketown. It illustrates his characteristic arrogance and obsession with his humble origins, showing how he boasts to visitors about his poor past while simultaneously displaying wealth through the property and its furnishings. The passage exemplifies Bounderby's hypocrisy and his tendency to use his former poverty as a tool for self-aggrandizement and social intimidation.
c20:p9: Mr. Bounderby is boasting to a visitor about his humble origins and his disdain for the expensive artwork in his country house, demonstrating his characteristic self-aggrandizing behavior by contrasting his past poverty with his current wealth.
c20:p10: This passage is Mr. Bounderby's boastful monologue to Mr. Harthouse at his country estate. Bounderby displays his characteristic self-aggrandizing behavior by contrasting his rise from poverty (sleeping in market baskets) with the fall of the previous owner, Nickits, who attended Westminster School and performed in classical plays but now lives in obscurity in Antwerp. The speech exemplifies Bounderby's vulgar pride in his material success and his obsession with his humble origins, while also revealing his callous indifference to others' misfortunes.
c20:p11: Mr. Harthouse, a charming but morally indifferent politician visiting Coketown, has been cultivating a relationship with Louisa Bounderby while staying at her husband's country estate. Having observed her beautiful face light up when speaking of her brother Tom, he now begins a deliberate campaign to seduce her by appealing to her maternal affection for Tom and her unhappiness in her marriage.
c20:p12: James Harthouse, a idle gentleman visiting Coketown, has been cultivating a relationship with Louisa Bounderby by gathering information about her from her brother Tom. He deliberately encounters Louisa alone in a secluded wooded area of her husband's estate to begin a direct seduction, using flattery about her brother to gain her trust.
c20:p13: Mr. Harthouse deliberately seeks out Louisa at her secluded spot in the woods, having learned her habits and routines. He plans to manipulate her emotionally by discussing her brother Tom's financial troubles and gambling debts, using her devotion to Tom as an opening to gain her confidence and drive a wedge between her and her husband.
c20:p14: Mr. Harthouse sits down beside Louisa in a secluded opening in the woods, where she habitually sits alone. This is the beginning of his deliberate attempt to seduce her by establishing an intimate conversation about her brother Tom's financial troubles and gambling debts, which he uses as a pretext to gain her confidence and emotional closeness.
c20:p15: Harthouse begins to seduce Louisa by using her affection for her brother Tom as an emotional lever, initiating a private conversation with her in a secluded woodland spot where he mentions Tom to capture her attention and sympathy.
c20:p16: James Harthouse, visiting the Bounderby estate, encounters Louisa alone in the woods and begins to seduce her by discussing her brother Tom's financial troubles. When he mentions Tom, Louisa's face lights up with sisterly concern, revealing an emotional depth that captivates Harthouse and confirms his manipulative strategy to exploit her affection for her brother as a means to draw her closer to him.
c20:p17: James Harthouse approaches Louisa in a secluded woodland opening and begins a calculated seduction. He initially addresses her concern for her brother Tom, praising her sisterly devotion while subtly manipulating her emotions to establish an intimate confidence between them that excludes her husband.
c20:p18: Louisa responds with composed indifference when Mr. Harthouse claims to be compelled to admire her sisterly affection for Tom, revealing her characteristic emotional restraint even as he begins his seduction through flattery and manipulation.
c20:p19: James Harthouse, a cynical gentleman visiting Coketown, encounters Louisa Bounderby alone in a wood and begins to manipulate her by discussing her brother Tom's financial troubles. When Louisa appears moved by his flattery about her sisterly devotion, Harthouse deflects by cynically disclaiming any pretense of virtue, openly admitting his self-interested nature as he attempts to establish an intimate confidence with her.

c9:p2: This passage appears in **[P2]** and serves as a key thematic reflection on the workers ("Hands") in the mill. The narrator argues that while engines are predictable, human souls contain unfathomable depths of potential for good or evil that cannot be quantified or managed through mere arithmetic. This meditation precedes Stephen Blackpool's introduction and establishes the novel's central tension between mechanization and human dignity.
c9:p3: This passage describes the industrial mill during midday, showing the continuation of factory work despite daylight breaking through. It follows Stephen Blackpool's morning labor at his loom and precedes the noon-bell that signals the workers' lunch break, emphasizing the relentless, polluted nature of the manufacturing environment in Coketown.
c9:p4: This chunk marks the midday break in the factory work at Coketown. It signals the transition point where Stephen Blackpool leaves his loom and walks to his employer Mr. Bounderby's house to seek advice about divorcing his alcoholic, abusive wife.
c9:p5: Stephen Blackpool, a weaver at Bounderby's mill, leaves his workplace during the noon break and travels to his employer's house to seek advice about obtaining a divorce from his alcoholic wife, who has recently returned to him.
c9:p6: Stephen Blackpool, a mill worker, arrives at his employer Mr. Bounderby's house during lunch to seek advice about how to divorce his alcoholic wife so he can marry another woman. This passage describes Stephen's arrival and the servant's announcement that allows him entry into Bounderby's presence.
c9:p7: Stephen Blackpool visits his employer Mr. Bounderby at his home to seek legal advice about divorcing his alcoholic wife. Upon entering the parlor, he finds Bounderby at lunch with his housekeeper Mrs. Sparsit present, who maintains an air of refined superiority throughout the conversation.
c9:p8: Stephen Blackpool, a mill worker, has come to Mr. Bounderby's house during lunch to seek advice about his troubled marriage. After being admitted to the parlor where Bounderby sits with Mrs. Sparsit, Bounderby opens the conversation with this question, initiating Stephen's explanation of his domestic troubles and his desire to be freed from his alcoholic wife.
c9:p9: Stephen Blackpool, a mill worker, visits his employer Mr. Bounderby at home to seek advice about his troubled marriage. Upon entering Bounderby's parlor, Stephen greets his employer with a respectful but not servile bow, adjusting his appearance out of deference to Mrs. Sparsit, Bounderby's housekeeper, before beginning to explain his domestic situation.
c9:p10: Stephen Blackpool, a mill worker, visits his employer Mr. Bounderby at home during lunch to seek advice about his troubled marriage. Before Stephen can explain his purpose, Bounderby preemptively dismisses the possibility that Stephen has come to complain, sarcastically suggesting that workers like him only desire luxuries like coaches and fancy food. Bounderby congratulates himself for knowing Stephen's character in advance, unaware of the serious personal crisis Stephen is about to disclose.
c9:p11: Stephen Blackpool responds to Mr. Bounderby's assumption that he has come to complain about his wages and working conditions, denying that this is his purpose for the visit.
c9:p12: Stephen Blackpool, a mill worker, visits his employer Mr. Bounderby at home during lunch to seek advice about his troubled marriage. After Stephen assures Bounderby that he hasn't come to complain about wages or working conditions, Bounderby responds with this passage, encouraging Stephen to explain the actual purpose of his visit.
c9:p13: Stephen Blackpool visits his employer Mr. Bounderby at his house to seek advice about his unhappy marriage. As Stephen is about to explain his situation in Bounderby's parlor, he glances toward Mrs. Sparsit, who is present at lunch. Mrs. Sparsit offers to leave the room if Stephen wishes to discuss something unsuitable for a lady to hear.
c9:p14: Stephen Blackpool visits his employer Mr. Bounderby's house to seek advice about divorcing his alcoholic wife. Mrs. Sparsit, Bounderby's housekeeper, offers to leave the room so Stephen can speak privately, but Bounderby insists she stay, assuring Stephen she is a "born lady." Stephen then begins recounting his marital troubles.
c9:p15: Stephen Blackpool, a mill worker, has come to Mr. Bounderby's house to seek advice on how to divorce his alcoholic, abusive wife so he can marry another woman. Before Stephen can fully explain his situation, Bounderby interrupts to assure Stephen that Mrs. Sparsit, his housekeeper, is a "born lady" of high social standing and may remain in the room during their conversation.
c9:p16: Stephen Blackpool, a factory worker, visits his employer Mr. Bounderby seeking advice on how to divorce his alcoholic wife so he can marry another woman. When Bounderby offers to let him speak freely, Stephen reassures him that he would never say anything inappropriate before a lady, responding with this modest and respectful statement to Mrs. Sparsit's presence in the room.
c9:p17: Stephen Blackpool, a factory worker, visits his employer Mr. Bounderby at home during lunch to seek advice about his situation. After brief introductions and Bounderby's confirmation that Stephen is not complaining about wanting luxuries, Bounderby invites him to speak freely about his problem.
c9:p18: Stephen Blackpool visits his employer Mr. Bounderby at home to seek advice about his marriage. After being admitted to the parlor where Bounderby is eating lunch with Mrs. Sparsit present, Stephen begins explaining his difficult domestic situation—he has been married for nineteen years to a woman who descended into alcoholism and dissolution, through no fault of his own, and he now seeks legal guidance on how to escape the marriage.
c9:p19: Stephen Blackpool has come to Mr. Bounderby's house seeking advice on how to be rid of his wife, who abandoned him years ago and has now returned. Stephen has just begun recounting his long history of suffering in his marriage, describing how his wife "went bad" early on. Bounderby interrupts to demonstrate he already knows the story, summarizing her descent into drinking and destitution in crude terms.
c9:p20: Stephen Blackpool is describing his long-suffering marriage to Mr. Bounderby, recounting how his wife descended into alcoholism and dissolution. When Bounderby interrupts to summarize her destructive behavior, Stephen responds with this line, emphasizing his endurance and forbearance despite her actions.
c9:p21: Stephen Blackpool confesses to his employer Mr. Bounderby about his troubled marriage, explaining how his wife took to drinking and abandoned their home. As Stephen describes his patience with her deteriorating behavior, Bounderby makes this dismissive aside to his wine glass, mocking Stephen's forbearance.
c9:p22: Stephen Blackpool recounts to his employer Mr. Bounderby his decades-long suffering in a disastrous marriage to a woman who became an alcoholic and squandered their household, describing his repeated failed attempts to reform her and the emotional devastation he endured.
c9:p23: Stephen Blackpool recounts his nineteen-year marriage to his wife, who became an alcoholic and dissolute, causing him immense suffering. As he describes the depths of his misery—finding her unconscious, contemplating suicide, paying her to stay away—his emotional anguish becomes physically visible in his face, betraying the torment he has endured.
c9:p24: Stephen Blackpool describes to his employer Mr. Bounderby the deterioration of his marriage and his wife's abandonment and repeated returns, explaining the emotional and physical toll it has taken on him—including his despair and suicidal thoughts—as he seeks advice on how to obtain a legal separation or divorce.
c9:p25: Stephen Blackpool has come to Mr. Bounderby's house to seek advice on how to divorce his alcoholic, abusive wife so he can marry another woman. As Stephen describes his nineteen years of suffering in his marriage, Mrs. Sparsit responds with this gesture, implying that people of her social station also experience hardship and deserve sympathy.
c9:p26: Stephen Blackpool, a mill worker, visits his employer Mr. Bounderby seeking advice on how to divorce his wife, who abandoned him years ago but has recently returned. In this passage, Stephen explains that he has paid his wife to stay away for the past five years, during which he has rebuilt his life respectably. However, she has now reappeared at his home, forcing him to confront his impossible situation under the law.
c9:p27: Stephen Blackpool, a factory worker, visits his employer Mr. Bounderby at home to seek advice on how to legally separate from his alcoholic and dissolute wife so he can marry another woman. This passage describes Stephen's physical demeanor as he recounts his years of suffering in the marriage—momentarily showing pride and passion before returning to his characteristic humble, contemplative posture while addressing his employer.
c9:p28: Stephen Blackpool has come to Mr. Bounderby seeking advice on how to divorce his wife, who has returned after years of abandonment and alcoholism. Blackpool explains his nineteen-year marriage and his suffering. Bounderby responds dismissively, saying he already knew the details of Stephen's marital troubles and suggests Stephen should never have married in the first place.
c9:p29: Mrs. Sparsit interrupts Stephen Blackpool's account of his unhappy marriage to Mr. Bounderby by asking whether the marriage was unequal in terms of the couple's ages, implying that a significant age difference might explain the marriage's misery.
c9:p30: Stephen Blackpool visits his employer Mr. Bounderby to seek advice on how to divorce his alcoholic, abusive wife so he can marry another woman. After Stephen explains his nineteen-year marriage has been miserable, Mrs. Sparsit asks whether the marriage was unequal in terms of age difference, and Bounderby repeats her question to Stephen.
c9:p31: Stephen Blackpool is speaking with his employer Mr. Bounderby about his unhappy marriage. When asked by Mrs. Sparsit whether his marriage was unequal in terms of age, Stephen responds that he and his wife were nearly the same age—he was twenty-one and she was twenty.
c9:p32: Stephen Blackpool visits his employer Mr. Bounderby to seek advice on how to divorce his alcoholic and abusive wife so he can marry another woman. Mrs. Sparsit, Bounderby's housekeeper, makes this comment when Stephen reveals that he and his wife were of nearly equal ages (both around twenty when married), contradicting her assumption that the marriage's misery stemmed from a significant age difference.
c9:p33: Stephen Blackpool has come to Mr. Bounderby seeking advice on how to obtain a divorce from his dissolute wife so he can marry another woman. Mrs. Sparsit, Bounderby's housekeeper, makes a pointed observation suggesting that Stephen's miserable marriage must be unequal in age—implying that he married beneath his station. Bounderby's uncomfortable reaction to her insinuation reveals his awareness that her comment has exposed a flaw in his earlier reasoning.
c9:p34: Stephen Blackpool has come to Mr. Bounderby's house seeking advice on how to divorce his wife, who has returned home after years of abandonment and degradation. After Stephen explains his long suffering marriage, Bounderby impatiently prompts him to continue with his request, as Stephen has paused before asking the crucial question about how to rid himself of his wife.
c9:p35: Stephen Blackpool, a mill worker, visits his employer Mr. Bounderby at home to seek advice about his marriage. After explaining his wife's years of alcoholism and abandonment, Stephen asks how he can be freed from her, expressing his desire to marry another woman. Mrs. Sparsit reacts with moral disapproval to his request for divorce.
c9:p36: Stephen Blackpool, a mill worker, visits his employer Mr. Bounderby seeking advice on how to divorce his alcoholic, abusive wife who has recently returned to their home. When Stephen asks how he can be "ridded of this woman" so he can marry another, Bounderby responds with this line, invoking the marriage vow "for better for worse" to refuse Stephen's request for help.
c9:p37: Stephen Blackpool, a weaver seeking divorce from his alcoholic wife, appeals to his employer Mr. Bounderby for legal advice on how to end his marriage. In this passage, Stephen expresses his desperation, explaining that he cannot endure his situation any longer and that only the comfort of another woman has prevented him from losing his mind.
c9:p38: Stephen Blackpool, a mill worker, visits his employer Mr. Bounderby to seek advice on how to escape his abusive marriage. After Stephen explains his wife's alcoholism and degradation, and expresses his desire to be free to marry another woman, Mrs. Sparsit makes this observation, interpreting Stephen's request as a wish to divorce and remarry.
c9:p39: Stephen Blackpool appeals to his employer Mr. Bounderby for legal advice on how to divorce his alcoholic, abusive wife so he can marry another woman. Stephen contrasts his situation with that of wealthy people who have the financial means and legal access to separate from unhappy marriages, while working-class people like himself have no such options despite facing equal or worse marital hardship.
c9:p40: Stephen Blackpool asks his employer Mr. Bounderby for legal advice on how to divorce his dissolute wife so he can marry another woman. Bounderby bluntly refuses, stating there is no way to help him, as divorce requires expensive legal proceedings through multiple courts costing a thousand to fifteen hundred pounds—far beyond Stephen's means as a factory worker.
c9:p41: Stephen Blackpool is appealing to his employer Mr. Bounderby for advice on how to divorce his alcoholic, abusive wife so he can marry another woman. When Bounderby offers no legal remedy, Stephen begins questioning what laws exist to address his situation, establishing the impossibility of escape from his marriage despite his suffering.
c9:p42: Stephen Blackpool questions Mr. Bounderby about the legal consequences of various actions regarding his unhappy marriage, asking if there are laws to punish him for hurting his wife, fleeing from her, remarrying, or living with another woman unmarried. Mr. Bounderby confirms the existence of such laws with this repeated response.
c9:p43: Stephen Blackpool asks Mr. Bounderby a series of rhetorical questions about the legal consequences of various options to escape his unhappy marriage to his alcoholic wife. This particular question concerns the legal punishment for abandoning her.
c9:p44: Stephen Blackpool asks Mr. Bounderby a series of questions about laws that would punish him for various ways of escaping his failed marriage. This response is Bounderby's repeated answer to Stephen's questions about whether there are laws against marrying another woman, fleeing, or living with another woman without marriage.
c9:p45: Stephen Blackpool is asking Mr. Bounderby about the legal consequences of his situation. Desperate to escape his abusive, alcoholic wife who has returned to him, Stephen seeks advice on how he might legally separate from her or marry another woman he loves. He questions what laws would punish him for various actions—hurting her, fleeing, or remarrying—revealing the impossible legal bind he faces as a working-class man without the wealth or social position that allows the rich to divorce and remarry.
c9:p46: Stephen Blackpool asks Mr. Bounderby a series of questions about the legal consequences of various actions regarding his unhappy marriage to his alcoholic wife. Each time he asks if there is a law to punish him for different scenarios (hurting her, fleeing, remarrying, or cohabiting without marriage), Bounderby repeatedly responds "Of course there is," emphasizing the legal constraints binding Stephen to his wife despite his desire to marry another woman.
c9:p47: Stephen Blackpool appeals to his employer Mr. Bounderby for legal advice on how to divorce his alcoholic, abusive wife so he can marry another woman. Stephen systematically asks about laws that would punish him for various options—hurting her, fleeing, remarrying—to illustrate that the law offers no path to freedom from his miserable marriage, even suggesting he could live with another woman without marriage, which would illegitimize their children.
c9:p48: Stephen Blackpool questions Mr. Bounderby about the legal consequences of various actions related to his unhappy marriage, asking if there are laws to punish him for hurting his wife, fleeing from her, remarrying, or living with another woman. Bounderby's repeated response "'Of course there is'" affirms the existence of punitive laws for each scenario, emphasizing the legal trap Stephen finds himself in.
c9:p49: Stephen Blackpool appeals to his employer Mr. Bounderby for help escaping his disastrous marriage to a woman who has abandoned herself to drinking and degradation. After Bounderby explains that divorce requires an expensive Act of Parliament costing thousands of pounds—accessible only to the wealthy—Stephen desperately pleads for some law to help him, highlighting the injustice that laws exist to punish the poor for their circumstances but none exist to help them.
c9:p50: Stephen Blackpool, a mill worker, visits his employer Mr. Bounderby seeking advice on how to obtain a divorce from his dissolute wife so he can marry another woman. After Stephen explains his years of suffering, Bounderby dismisses the possibility, stating that marriage must be maintained as a sacred institution, despite the law's prohibitive cost and inflexibility.
c9:p51: Stephen Blackpool appeals to Mr. Bounderby for legal advice on how to divorce his alcoholic, abusive wife so he can marry another woman. When Bounderby dismisses the matter by invoking the sanctity of marriage, Stephen passionately argues that the law's prohibition on divorce traps working-class people in miserable marriages, unlike the wealthy who can separate, and that this impossibility drives ordinary people to violence and murder. He pleads to know what law exists to help him escape his situation.
c9:p52: Stephen Blackpool has come to Mr. Bounderby asking for legal advice on how to obtain a divorce from his dissolute wife so he can marry another woman. After Stephen's emotional appeal detailing his wife's alcoholism and abandonment, Bounderby dismisses the possibility, saying there is no law to help him. Stephen despairs that it is "a muddle." Bounderby then reconsiders and makes this statement, offering hope that such a law does exist, though he immediately qualifies it by noting its extreme cost.
c9:p53: Stephen Blackpool has just learned from Mr. Bounderby that there is a law allowing divorce, but only for the wealthy at great expense (one to fifteen hundred pounds). Stephen, who sought advice on how to free himself from his alcoholic wife so he could marry another woman, accepts this information with quiet resignation before learning the law is beyond his means.
c9:p54: Stephen Blackpool asks Mr. Bounderby how he can be legally freed from his wife to marry another woman. Bounderby tells him there is a law permitting divorce, but it is prohibitively expensive.
c9:p55: Stephen Blackpool visits his employer Mr. Bounderby to seek advice on how to divorce his estranged, alcoholic wife so he can marry another woman. When Bounderby reveals that divorce requires an expensive legal process costing a thousand to fifteen hundred pounds, Stephen asks how much money that would be, as he cannot afford such a sum.
c9:p56: Stephen Blackpool seeks Mr. Bounderby's advice on how to divorce his alcoholic, abusive wife so he can marry another woman. Bounderby explains the prohibitively expensive legal process required to obtain a parliamentary divorce, revealing that it would cost Stephen between one thousand and fifteen hundred pounds—an impossibly large sum for a factory worker.
c9:p57: Stephen Blackpool asks Mr. Bounderby about the legal options for divorce. After learning that divorce requires going through Doctors' Commons, Common Law courts, the House of Lords, and an Act of Parliament at a cost of £1,000-£1,500, Stephen desperately asks if there is any other legal avenue available to him.
c9:p58: Stephen Blackpool asks Mr. Bounderby if there is any other legal way besides an expensive parliamentary act to divorce his wife. Bounderby's curt reply "'Certainly not'" closes off any alternative options, leaving Stephen trapped in an unhappy marriage due to the prohibitive cost of legal separation.
c9:p59: Stephen Blackpool, a factory worker, visits his employer Mr. Bounderby to ask for legal advice on how to divorce his wife, who has abandoned him and returned destitute. After explaining his years of suffering, Bounderby informs him that divorce requires an Act of Parliament and costs between one thousand and fifteen hundred pounds—an impossibly large sum for a working man. Facing this insurmountable legal and financial barrier, Stephen despairingly concludes that the system is fundamentally unjust.
c9:p60: Stephen Blackpool asks his employer Mr. Bounderby how he can divorce his wife to marry another woman. When Stephen expresses despair about the expensive legal process (costing £1000-£1500), he calls the situation "a muddle." Mrs. Sparsit is shocked and dismayed by what she views as his impious and immoral sentiments, reflecting her disapproval of the working-class perspective on marriage and divorce law.
c9:p61: Stephen Blackpool has come to Mr. Bounderby's house to seek advice on how to legally separate from his alcoholic wife, whom he has supported for years. After Stephen explains his miserable marriage and argues that the poor should have access to divorce like the wealthy do, Bounderby dismisses his plea, tells him divorce is prohibitively expensive, and then responds with this passage, where he dismisses Stephen's criticism of the country's institutions as nonsense and insists Stephen simply accept his marital situation and focus on his factory work.
c9:p62: Stephen Blackpool, a factory worker, has just visited his employer Mr. Bounderby to ask for legal advice on how to divorce his alcoholic wife so he can marry another woman. When Bounderby explains that divorce requires an expensive Act of Parliament costing thousands of pounds—an impossibility for a poor worker—Stephen expresses his frustration with the injustice of the law that allows the wealthy to divorce easily while trapping the poor in unhappy marriages. His repeated declaration that everything is "a muddle" reflects his despair at the contradictory and unfair legal system.
c9:p63: Stephen Blackpool visits Mr. Bounderby seeking legal advice on how to divorce his dissolute wife so he can marry another woman. After Stephen explains his years of suffering and asks what law might help him, Bounderby dismisses him by claiming divorce requires an Act of Parliament costing thousands of pounds—far beyond a working man's means. As Stephen leaves, Bounderby delivers this parting rebuke, accusing him of holding "unhallowed opinions" and suggesting he has been corrupted by outside agitators rather than accepting his station and marital obligations.
c9:p64: Stephen Blackpool, a weaver, visits his employer Mr. Bounderby to seek advice on how to obtain a divorce from his alcoholic and unfaithful wife so he can marry another woman. Bounderby explains that divorce requires expensive legal proceedings costing thousands of pounds, which Stephen cannot afford. Frustrated by the impossibility of his situation, Stephen declares the system "a muddle." Bounderby dismisses his concerns and warns him against listening to troublemakers, accusing him of wanting luxuries. Stephen then departs, departing with resignation while Bounderby remains self-satisfied.
